tasks.content: A வாதம்/விவாதம் (vaadham/vivaadham, debate) is a structured discussion in which speakers argue for or against a given statement, called a தீர்மானம் (theermaanam, motion). To take a clear stance, you might open with "என் கருத்துப்படி..." (en karuthuppadi, "in my opinion...") before stating your position, then give a காரணம் (kaaranam, reason) to support it — for example, "ஏனெனில்..." (yenenil, "because..."). Debaters are generally split into ஆதரவு (aadaravu, those in favour/support) and எதிர்ப்பு (edhirppu, those opposed), and each side takes turns presenting points within a set time. Learning to state an opinion clearly and back it with a reason is the essential first skill of Tamil debate.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Translating between Tamil and English builds a deeper understanding of both languages by forcing you to notice differences in word order and sentence structure. Tamil typically follows a subject-object-verb order, so "நான் பள்ளிக்குச் செல்கிறேன்" (naan pallikku selgiren) word-for-word is "I to-school am-going," which becomes natural English as "I am going to school." Going the other direction, the English sentence "The sky is blue" becomes "வானம் நீலமானது" (vaanam neelamaanadhu) in Tamil, where the verb "is" is expressed through the adjective ending -ானது rather than a separate word. Good translators aim for sentences that sound natural in the target language, not just a literal word-for-word swap.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: யாப்பு (yaappu) is the traditional system of Tamil poetic meter, built from small units that combine into larger ones like building blocks. The smallest unit above a single letter is the அசை (asai, metrical syllable), of which there are two kinds: நேரசை (neerasai, a single long unit) and நிரையசை (niraiyasai, a double short unit). Several asai combine to form a சீர் (seer, metrical foot), several seer combine to form an அடி (adi, a line of verse), and the linking pattern between feet is governed by rules called தளை (thalai). Understanding this ladder — எழுத்து (letter) to அசை (syllable) to சீர் (foot) to அடி (line) — is the foundation for reading and appreciating classical Tamil poetry such as the Thirukkural and Sangam verses.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Studying a novel in depth means tracing how theme, character and historical context interweave across the whole text, not just a single chapter. A character's development often mirrors or challenges a novel's central themes, and understanding when and where a novel was written, its historical context, reveals why certain issues, such as war, class or industrial change, dominate the story. Strong analysis tracks how an author builds a theme gradually, using specific moments and quotations from across the novel rather than relying on a single scene.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Studying a full Shakespeare play means tracking how plot, character and language develop across five acts, not just an isolated extract. Shakespeare often builds character through soliloquy — a speech where a character speaks their inner thoughts alone on stage — revealing motivations the other characters cannot see. Tracing how a character's language changes across the play, in vocabulary, imagery or verse pattern, can reveal their psychological journey, such as a descent into guilt or a rise to power, and understanding the play's structure of acts and scenes shows how tension builds towards its climax.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A complex sentence combines a main clause, which can stand alone, with one or more subordinate clauses, which cannot, joined by subordinating conjunctions such as 'although,' 'because,' 'while' or 'since.' Subordination lets a writer show precise relationships between ideas — cause and effect, contrast, or condition — rather than simply listing them with 'and.' Where a subordinate clause is placed matters too: a fronted subordinate clause, at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma, can create emphasis or suspense before the main point arrives.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Every genre carries its own conventions — recognisable features readers expect. Horror relies on building dread through pacing, sensory detail and the unknown; mystery plants clues and red herrings so a reader can almost solve the puzzle alongside the detective; and science fiction extrapolates real science or technology into speculative 'what if' worlds, often to comment on present-day society. Writing convincingly within a genre means deliberately using its conventions — vocabulary, structure, pacing and typical character types — while still creating something original rather than a cliche.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Gothic fiction creates unease through atmosphere as much as plot, typically featuring decaying settings, such as crumbling castles or gloomy mansions, oppressive weather, and a sense of the supernatural or uncanny threatening rational order. Writers build tension through pathetic fallacy, where weather reflects mood, foreshadowing, and withheld information that keeps readers uncertain about what is real. Studying a Gothic extract means tracing exactly how setting, structure and word choice combine to unsettle the reader, rather than simply noting 'it's scary.'

tasks.content: Media literacy means reading news and online content critically, recognising that no source is entirely neutral: headline choice, image selection, which quotations are included, and even word choice, such as 'rioters' versus 'protesters,' can all reveal a publication's bias. Checking a source's ownership, funding and typical audience, and comparing how different outlets report the same story, helps readers spot one-sided reporting and distinguish verified fact from unchecked claims or opinion presented as fact. Being media-literate does not mean distrusting everything — it means questioning and cross-checking before accepting a claim.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A strong argumentative essay states a clear thesis, the writer's central position, in the introduction, then develops distinct points in separate paragraphs, each supported by evidence and explained rather than simply asserted. tasks.content: World literature broadens a reader's understanding beyond the British literary canon, exploring how writers from different countries and cultures use story to explore universal themes — identity, family, conflict, belonging — while also reflecting their own specific cultural and historical context. Reading in translation raises its own questions: a translator makes deliberate choices about word choice, idiom and rhythm, meaning that a translated text carries both the original author's voice and the translator's interpretation. Approaching a text from an unfamiliar culture with curiosity, and researching its context, deepens understanding rather than assuming it works exactly like a familiar British text.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Two quantities are in direct proportion if their ratio stays constant, so if y = kx and we know one pair of values we can find k and use it to find others. Two quantities are in inverse proportion if one increases as the other decreases, so xy = k stays constant. For example, if y is directly proportional to x and y = 12 when x = 4, then k = 3, so when x = 9, y = 27.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In a right-angled triangle, Pythagoras' theorem states that a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse (the longest side, opposite the right angle). To find the hypotenuse, square both shorter sides, add them, then square root: legs of 3 and 4 give a hypotenuse of the square root of (9 + 16) = the square root of 25 = 5. To find a shorter side, rearrange: square the hypotenuse, subtract the known side squared, then square root.

tasks.content: The digestive system breaks down food into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood and used by the body for energy, growth and repair. Digestion begins in the mouth, where chewing and saliva start to break down food, continues in the stomach with acid and enzymes, and is completed in the small intestine, where enzymes finish breaking down food and nutrients are absorbed through finger-like projections called villi. Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up digestion: amylase breaks down starch into sugars, protease breaks down proteins into amino acids, and lipase breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

tasks.content: In a chemical reaction, the atoms in the reactants are rearranged to form new substances called products, with new chemical bonds forming; importantly, atoms are never created or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same, which is known as the law of conservation of mass. Many reactions involve an energy change: exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings, often as heat, causing the temperature to rise, while endothermic reactions absorb energy, causing the temperature to fall. Chemical reactions can be represented using word equations and balanced symbol equations, which show exactly how many atoms of each element are involved on both sides.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Electric current is the flow of electrical charge around a circuit, measured in amperes (amps, A) with an ammeter, while voltage (potential difference), measured in volts with a voltmeter, is the energy transferred per unit of charge that pushes the current around. Magnets have two poles, north and south, and like poles repel while opposite poles attract, with the invisible magnetic field around a magnet mapped using field lines that run from north to south. An electric current flowing through a wire creates a magnetic field around it, and this effect, called electromagnetism, is used to make electromagnets, which are magnets that can be switched on and off using electricity.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: An ecosystem is made up of all the living organisms (the community) in an area interacting with each other and with the non-living parts of their environment, such as soil, water and climate. Within an ecosystem, organisms depend on one another through feeding relationships shown in food chains and food webs, where energy passes from producers (usually plants, which make their own food by photosynthesis) to primary consumers, then secondary and tertiary consumers. This interdependence means that a change affecting one species, such as a predator being removed, can have knock-on effects throughout the whole food web, which is why maintaining balanced ecosystems is important.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: The periodic table arranges all known elements in order of increasing atomic number, into rows called periods and columns called groups, with elements in the same group sharing similar chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell. Metals, found on the left and centre of the table, are typically shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, and malleable, while non-metals, found on the right, are generally dull, brittle if solid, and poor conductors. Group 1 elements, the alkali metals, are very reactive and get more reactive down the group, while Group 0, the noble gases, are extremely unreactive because they already have full outer electron shells.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Energy resources are used to generate the electricity and power we rely on, and are grouped into renewable resources, which are naturally replenished and will not run out, such as solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal and geothermal, and non-renewable resources, such as coal, oil and natural gas (fossil fuels) and nuclear fuel, which exist in limited amounts and cannot be quickly replaced. Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide when burned, contributing to climate change, while most renewable resources produce little or no carbon dioxide during use but can be less reliable, such as solar power depending on sunlight. Choosing energy resources involves weighing up factors like cost, reliability, environmental impact and how much energy each resource can supply.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Light and sound both travel as waves, but light is a transverse wave that can travel through a vacuum (such as space) at very high speed, while sound is a longitudinal wave caused by vibrations, which needs a medium like air, water or a solid to travel through, and travels much more slowly. Waves are described using amplitude (the maximum displacement, related to loudness for sound or brightness for light), wavelength (the distance between two matching points on a wave), and frequency (the number of waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz), linked by the wave equation: wave speed = frequency × wavelength. Higher frequency sound waves are heard as higher pitch, while for light, higher frequency corresponds to a different colour, towards the violet/blue end of the visible spectrum.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Metals can be arranged in order of their reactivity, called the reactivity series, which helps predict how they will behave in reactions: more reactive metals, such as potassium and sodium, react vigorously, while less reactive metals, such as gold and copper, are largely unreactive. Many metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, react with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas (more readily for reactive metals), and react with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas. A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound in a displacement reaction, which is further evidence used to build up the reactivity series.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food, using energy from light to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen; it takes place mainly in the chloroplasts of leaf cells, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light energy. Respiration, in contrast, occurs in all living cells and releases energy from glucose for the organism to use; aerobic respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water, while anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen and, in animal cells, produces lactic acid instead. Photosynthesis and respiration are essentially opposite processes, and together they play a key role in maintaining the balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Evaluating an investigation means critically reviewing how well the method worked and how confident you can be in the results, rather than simply describing what was done. This includes identifying sources of error, such as random errors (small, unpredictable variations, reduced by repeating measurements and averaging) and systematic errors (a consistent bias, often caused by a fault in equipment such as an incorrectly zeroed balance, which shifts every reading in the same direction). A good evaluation also considers the investigation's reliability (whether repeating it gives consistent results) and validity (whether it actually tests what it claims to, with all other variables properly controlled), and suggests specific, practical improvements.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: புணர்ச்சி (puṇarcci, sandhi) refers to the rules governing how sounds change when two words are joined together in Tamil, similar to how English "do not" becomes "don't." A common example is "மழை" (mazhai, rain) combining with "காலம்" (kaalam, season/time) to form the compound "மழைக்காலம்" (mazhaikkaalam, "rainy season"), where a hard க் sound is inserted at the join. Traditional grammar sorts these changes into categories such as உயிர்த் தொடர் புணர்ச்சி (vowel-to-vowel sandhi), மெய்த் தொடர் புணர்ச்சி (consonant-to-consonant sandhi) and உயிர்மெய்த் தொடர் புணர்ச்சி (mixed sandhi). Recognising sandhi patterns helps you correctly split unfamiliar compound words back into their original parts when reading classical or formal Tamil.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Inbam Pal (இன்பத்துப்பால், also called காமத்துப்பால், Kaamathuppaal) is the third and final section of the Thirukkural, containing 250 couplets across 25 chapters devoted to the theme of இன்பம் (inbam, love). Unlike Aram Pal's ethical teachings or Porul Pal's public-life advice, this section is written as an intimate dialogue between a தலைவன் (thalaivan, hero/lover) and தலைவி (thalaivi, heroine/beloved), exploring courtship, longing, separation and reunion much like the akam poetry of the Sangam tradition. Its verses capture universal emotional experiences of romantic love — the shyness of first attraction, the ache of a lover's absence, the joy of reconciliation — in the same tightly structured two-line kural form used throughout the work. Studying Inbam Pal shows how classical Tamil literature treats love with the same careful craftsmanship as ethics and politics.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Continuing beyond the idioms of Grade 6, this unit introduces more marabuthodar (மரபுத்தொடர், idioms) alongside அணி (ani, figures of speech) used to make Tamil expressive. "கை கழுவிவிடுதல்" (kai kazhuvividudhal), literally "to wash one's hands of it," means to completely disown responsibility for something. "நாக்கைக் கடித்துக் கொள்ளுதல்" (naakkai kadithuk kolludhal), literally "to bite one's own tongue," describes the moment of regret right after realising you said something you shouldn't have. Alongside idioms, Tamil poetry uses அணி such as உவமை அணி (uvamai ani, simile), as in "நிலா போன்ற முகம்" (a face like the moon), which directly compares two things using "போன்ற" (like/similar to).
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: This unit follows the central story of Silappathikaram in detail: Kannagi (கண்ணகி) and her husband Kovalan (கோவலன்) are a young married couple from Puhar, but Kovalan falls for a dancer named Madhavi (மாதவி) and squanders his fortune on her before returning, penniless, to Kannagi. The couple travels to Madurai to rebuild their lives, and Kannagi gives Kovalan her silambu (சிலம்பு, anklet) to sell — but he is wrongly accused of stealing the queen's anklet, which looks similar, and is unjustly executed by order of the Pandya king. Grief-stricken, Kannagi marches to the royal court and proves her husband's innocence by breaking open her remaining anklet: hers contains rubies, while the queen's contained pearls. In her fury at this injustice, Kannagi curses the city of Madurai, and this dramatic episode — Kannagi's grief turning to righteous anger — remains one of the most powerful moments in classical Tamil literature.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Kamba Ramayanam (கம்ப ராமாயணம்), also known as Ramavataram (இராமாவதாரம்), is the celebrated Tamil retelling of the Ramayana epic, composed by the poet Kambar (கம்பர்) around the 12th century CE. While it follows the same core story as Valmiki's Sanskrit Ramayana — Prince Rama's exile, the abduction of his wife Sita by the demon king Ravana, and the eventual war to rescue her — Kambar reshaped the narrative with rich Tamil poetic style, elaborate imagery and emotional depth suited to a Tamil audience of his era. The work is composed in thousands of verses across multiple kandams (books), and Kambar is often praised as one of the greatest poets in the Tamil literary tradition for the sheer craftsmanship of his verse. Kamba Ramayanam remains one of the most celebrated long narrative poems in Tamil literature, distinct in style and detail from its Sanskrit source.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Writing persuasively about a சமூகப் பிரச்சனை (samoogap pirachanai, social issue) means going beyond simple description to build an argument the reader can be convinced by. Choose a real topic such as சுற்றுச்சூழல் பாதுகாப்பு (environmental protection) or கல்வியின் முக்கியத்துவம் (the importance of education), then open with a clear thesis stating your position on it. Each body paragraph should present one piece of evidence or reasoning — a statistic, an example, or a logical argument — that directly supports that thesis, rather than simply listing loosely related facts. A strong persuasive essay on a social issue also briefly acknowledges an opposing view before explaining why your position remains stronger, which shows the reader you have thought the issue through carefully.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Building on the introduction to debate from Grade 6, this unit practises the formal roles and structure used in a organised Tamil வாதப் போட்டி (vaadhap potti, debate competition). Each side has a முன்மொழிபவர் (munmozhibavar, proposer) who opens the case, and speakers alternate presenting points within a strict கால வரம்பு (kaala varambu, time limit) enforced by a நடுவர் (naduvar, judge/adjudicator). A well-prepared formal debater doesn't just state opinions but organises them into a clear கட்டமைப்பு (kattamaippu, structure) — point, evidence, and a brief rebuttal of the opposing side's likely argument — delivered confidently within the time allowed. Practising this formal structure under timed conditions builds the confidence needed for real competitive debating.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Advanced translation goes beyond simple sentences to tackle idiomatic expressions, where a literal, word-for-word translation would sound strange or lose the original meaning entirely. For example, the Tamil proverb "கிணற்றுத் தவளைக்குக் கடல் தெரியுமா?" should not be translated literally as "does the well's frog know the ocean" but rendered with its equivalent English idiom, "like a frog in a well," to preserve the intended meaning for an English reader. Similarly, translating longer, more complex sentences requires reordering clauses — a Tamil sentence with a relative participle (பெயரெச்சம்) placed before a noun, like "நேற்று வந்த மாணவன்" (the student who came yesterday), must be restructured into an English relative clause with "who," since English cannot place a whole clause directly before a noun in the same way. Skilled translators balance staying faithful to the original meaning with producing natural, fluent sentences in the target language.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Puthukavithai (புதுக்கவிதை, "new poetry") is the modern free-verse movement in Tamil poetry that emerged in the 20th century as a deliberate break from the strict yaappu (poetic meter) rules that had shaped Tamil verse for centuries. Instead of fixed metrical patterns and rhyme, puthukavithai poets write in free verse, using natural rhythms of spoken Tamil, everyday vocabulary and contemporary themes — city life, personal emotion, social commentary — that older classical forms rarely addressed directly. This shift mirrors similar free-verse movements in other world literatures, where poets prioritised emotional directness and thematic freedom over rigid formal constraints. Reading puthukavithai alongside classical Sangam or Thirukkural verse highlights just how dramatically Tamil poetic form has evolved while the language itself remains continuous.

tasks.content: At the highest level, creative writing is a series of deliberate choices: every word, and every sentence's length and structure, should be chosen for a specific effect rather than habit. Precise verbs and concrete nouns, such as 'the branch snapped' rather than 'something happened,' create sharper images than vague, general language, while sentence length can be manipulated to control pacing — a sudden short sentence after a long, flowing one can land like a physical jolt. Strong writers redraft deliberately, questioning each word choice: does this verb, this rhythm, this structure serve the effect I want the reader to feel?

tasks.content: Transactional writing produces a text with a genuine real-world purpose and audience — a formal letter of complaint, a speech to persuade an audience, or a magazine article to inform and entertain — and each form has its own conventions of layout, tone and structure. Real-life graphs such as distance-time graphs also carry meaning: a horizontal section means the object is stationary, and the gradient of a sloped section represents speed.

tasks.content: Genetic information is stored in the nucleus of a cell in structures called chromosomes, made of a molecule called DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid), which is coiled into a double helix shape; sections of DNA that code for particular characteristics are called genes. Humans have 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs in most body cells, having inherited one chromosome of each pair from each parent, while cells divide by mitosis to produce two identical new cells for growth and repair. Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, which can have different versions called alleles, and whether a dominant or recessive allele is expressed determines the characteristic (phenotype) an organism shows.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Atoms are made of three types of subatomic particle: protons and neutrons, which have relatively large mass and are found in the central nucleus, and electrons, which have almost no mass and orbit the nucleus in shells (energy levels); protons carry a positive charge, electrons a negative charge, and neutrons no charge, and in a neutral atom the number of protons equals the number of electrons. The number of protons in an atom is its atomic number, which identifies the element, while the total number of protons and neutrons is its mass number. Atoms bond together in different ways: ionic bonding involves the transfer of electrons between a metal and a non-metal to form charged ions that attract each other, covalent bonding involves non-metal atoms sharing pairs of electrons, and metallic bonding involves a lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalised electrons.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Pressure is the force acting per unit area, calculated with the formula pressure = force ÷ area, and measured in pascals (Pa); this is why a sharp knife (small area) cuts more easily than a blunt one with the same force, and why wide skis spread a person's weight over a larger area to reduce pressure on snow. Pressure in a fluid, such as in a liquid, increases with depth because of the increasing weight of fluid above, and acts equally in all directions at a given point. Newton's laws of motion describe how forces affect movement: an object stays still or moves at a constant speed unless acted on by an unbalanced force (Newton's first law), and the resultant force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration, F = ma (Newton's second law).
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: The rate of a chemical reaction describes how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed, and can be increased by raising the temperature (giving particles more energy so they collide more often and harder), increasing the concentration of a solution or the pressure of a gas (making collisions more frequent), increasing the surface area of a solid reactant (exposing more particles to collide with), or adding a catalyst, which speeds up a reaction without being used up itself. This is explained by collision theory: for a reaction to happen, particles must collide with enough energy, called the activation energy, and more frequent or more energetic collisions lead to a faster reaction rate. Rate of reaction can be measured experimentally, for example by timing how long it takes for a fixed amount of gas to be produced, or by measuring how a reaction mixture's mass or appearance changes over time.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Homeostasis is the regulation of the internal conditions of the body, such as temperature, water content and blood glucose levels, to maintain a stable internal environment despite changes outside the body. The nervous system detects and responds to changes (stimuli) rapidly using electrical signals: receptors detect a stimulus, sensory neurones carry signals to the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), which processes information and sends signals along motor neurones to effectors, such as muscles or glands, which produce a response. A reflex is an automatic, rapid response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought, protecting the body from harm, such as pulling your hand away from something hot.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Electrical power is the rate at which energy is transferred, measured in watts (W), and can be calculated using the equation power = voltage × current (P = V × I); a higher-power appliance transfers more energy every second. In a series circuit, current is the same at every point and the total voltage is shared between components, whereas in a parallel circuit, the voltage across each branch is the same, but the current is shared between branches, so removing one component does not stop current flowing through the others. Energy transferred by an electrical appliance can be calculated using energy = power × time, which is how domestic electricity bills, based on the number of kilowatt-hours used, are calculated.

tasks.content: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon-based compounds, most of which are found in or derived from living things or fossil fuels; carbon atoms can form up to four covalent bonds, allowing them to build long chains and rings, giving rise to a huge variety of organic molecules. Hydrocarbons are compounds made only of hydrogen and carbon atoms, and crude oil is a mixture of many different hydrocarbons, most of which belong to a family called alkanes; alkanes have the general formula CnH2n+2 and contain only single bonds between carbon atoms, making them relatively unreactive (saturated). Crude oil is separated into more useful fractions, such as petrol, diesel and kerosene, by fractional distillation, which separates hydrocarbons based on their different boiling points.

tasks.content: The electromagnetic spectrum is a continuous range of transverse waves, all travelling at the same speed through a vacuum, arranged in order of increasing frequency (and energy) and decreasing wavelength: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Different parts of the spectrum have different uses because of how they interact with matter: radio waves are used for broadcasting, microwaves for cooking and satellite communication, infrared for thermal imaging and remote controls, ultraviolet causes sunburn and vitamin D production in skin, and X-rays and gamma rays, which are the highest-energy, most penetrating waves, are used for medical imaging and treating cancer, though excessive exposure can damage living cells and cause harm such as cancer.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Biodiversity is the variety of different species of living organisms found in an ecosystem or on Earth as a whole, and high biodiversity generally makes ecosystems more stable and resilient to change, because there are more alternative food sources and relationships if one species is affected. Human activities, such as deforestation, pollution, overfishing and climate change, are reducing biodiversity around the world, which is why conservation efforts, including protected nature reserves, captive breeding programmes and controls on hunting or land use, are used to try to protect and restore species and habitats. Ecologists study ecosystems using sampling techniques, such as quadrats to estimate population sizes of plants or slow-moving animals in an area, and transects to see how species distribution changes across an environment.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Survey of Tamil Literary History
tasks.content: Tamil literature spans one of the longest continuous literary traditions in the world, and this unit surveys its major eras in order. It begins with சங்க இலக்கியம் (Sangam literature), the earliest surviving poetry from roughly the last centuries BCE onward, followed by the post-Sangam era of the ஐம்பெருங்காப்பியங்கள் (Five Great Epics), which includes Silappathikaram, Manimekalai, Jivaka Chintamani, Valayapathi and Kundalakesi. Next came பக்தி இலக்கியம் (Bhakti literature), a great flowering of devotional poetry and hymns addressed to Shiva and Vishnu, composed by poet-saints over several centuries of the medieval period. The survey concludes with நவீன இலக்கியம் (modern literature), which grew from the 19th and 20th centuries onward to include novels, short stories and free-verse poetry such as puthukavithai, reflecting contemporary Tamil life and thought.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: செந்தமிழ் (sendhamizh, classical/literary Tamil) and கொடுந்தமிழ் (kodundhamizh, colloquial/spoken Tamil) represent two related but distinct registers of the same language. Classical Tamil preserves older grammatical forms and full spellings closer to traditional rules, as in the literary "செல்கின்றேன்" (I am going), while everyday spoken Tamil often contracts and simplifies this to "போறேன்" in casual conversation. These differences extend beyond single words to sentence structure, vocabulary choices and regional dialect variation, meaning a formal written essay and a casual chat between friends can sound almost like different varieties of the same language. Recognising when to use each register — formal literary Tamil for essays, exams and formal speech, versus natural colloquial Tamil for everyday conversation — is an important skill for any confident Tamil speaker and writer.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Advanced argumentative essay writing builds on basic essay structure by adding an எதிர்வாதம் (edhirvaadham, counter-argument) and பதிலுரை (padhilurai, rebuttal) to strengthen the writer's overall position. After presenting your main thesis and supporting evidence, a strong advanced essay dedicates a paragraph to fairly stating the strongest opposing argument, introduced with a phrase like "சிலர் கருதலாம்..." (some may argue that...), before directly countering it with reasoning or evidence in the rebuttal that follows. This structure — thesis, evidence, counter-argument, rebuttal, conclusion — shows a more sophisticated command of argument than simply repeating one's own view, and mirrors how mature persuasive writing works in any language. A strong concluding paragraph then reasserts the thesis in light of the rebuttal, leaving the reader with a clear, well-supported final impression.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: பொதுப் பேச்சு (podhup pechu, public speaking) and சொற்பொழிவு (sorpozhivu, formal oratory) are valued skills in Tamil culture, where confident, expressive speech has long been prized in gatherings, festivals and civic life. Effective public speaking blends clear content with delivery: varying your pace and tone (குரல் ஏற்ற இறக்கம், voice modulation) to hold an audience's attention, pausing for emphasis before an important point, and using rhetorical techniques such as repeating a phrase for impact. A speaker should also read and adapt to their audience — a school assembly speech calls for a different tone than a formal debate — while maintaining clear, well-organised content throughout, from a strong opening that captures attention to a memorable closing line. Practising aloud, not just writing a speech on paper, is essential to becoming a confident public speaker.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: இலக்கிய விமர்சனம் (ilakkiya vimarsanam, literary criticism) is the practice of analysing a text thoughtfully rather than simply summarising its plot. A literary critic examines கருப்பொருள் (karupporul, theme, the central idea or message a work explores), நடை (nadai, style, the particular way an author uses language and form), and பாத்திரப் படைப்பு (paathirap padaippu, characterisation, how believably and vividly characters are built). Critics also consider the ஆசிரியரின் நோக்கம் (aasiriyarin nokkam, the author's purpose) — why a text was written and what effect it seems designed to have on its reader. Applying these four lenses — theme, style, characterisation and purpose — to a Sangam poem, a Thirukkural couplet or a modern short story reveals layers of meaning that a first, surface-level reading often misses.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Comparative literature places texts from different languages and cultures side by side to notice shared human themes as well as culturally distinct approaches. For example, the Thirukkural's short, universal couplets of ethical wisdom can be compared with Aesop's Fables from ancient Greek tradition — both use compact, memorable forms to teach moral lessons, though the Thirukkural relies on direct statement while Aesop's fables use animal characters and allegory. Similarly, Kamba Ramayanam and an English epic poem like Milton's Paradise Lost can be compared as heroic, morally serious long narrative poems rooted in religious tradition, even though one retells a Hindu epic and the other a Christian one. This kind of comparison sharpens your understanding of each text individually, by asking what is universal about storytelling and morality across cultures, and what is shaped by each culture's particular tradition.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: This capstone grammar unit reviews and connects the major structures studied across earlier years into one advanced picture of Tamil sentence-building. It revisits வேற்றுமை (vetrumai, case markers) that show a noun's role, காலம் (kaalam, tense) that shows when an action happens, and the two participle forms — வினையெச்சம் (adverbial participle, linking sequential actions) and பெயரெச்சம் (adjectival participle, describing a noun) — that let Tamil build complex sentences without separate relative-clause words. It also reviews புணர்ச்சி (sandhi, the rules for sound changes where words join). Seeing all of these features working together in one advanced sentence, such as "நேற்று பள்ளிக்குச் சென்ற மாணவன் இன்று வீட்டில் படித்துக் கொண்டிருக்கிறான்" (the student who went to school yesterday is studying at home today), shows how Tamil grammar builds meaning through layered suffixes and participles rather than many separate small words.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Writing a சிறுகதை (sirukadhai, short story) in Tamil draws on the same core elements as short fiction in any language: பாத்திரம் (paathiram, character), களம் (kalam, setting) and கதைச்சுருக்கம் (kadhaichchurukkam, plot). A strong short story establishes its characters and setting efficiently within the opening lines, then builds a single clear conflict or turning point rather than trying to cram in too many events. Natural-sounding உரையாடல் (uraiyaadal, dialogue) brings characters to life — using colloquial spoken Tamil for dialogue, even within an otherwise more literary narration, often makes characters feel more real and relatable to the reader. Revising your own creative writing by reading it aloud is a useful way to check whether the dialogue and pacing feel natural.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: ஆய்வுத் திறன்கள் (aaivuth thiranghal, research skills) begin with gathering reliable ஆதாரங்கள் (aadhaarangal, sources) on a topic and taking clear notes rather than copying text directly. When you use another person's words or ideas, proper practice requires a மேற்கோள் (merkol, citation) acknowledging where the information came from, both to give credit fairly and to let others check your sources. Once research is gathered, organising it into a clear விளக்கக்காட்சி (vilakkakkaatchi, presentation) means structuring your findings logically — an introduction to the topic, a few clearly organised main points, and a conclusion — and supporting your spoken explanation with well-chosen காட்சிப் பொருள்கள் (kaatchip porulgal, visual aids) such as images, charts or key words on a slide, rather than dense blocks of text the audience must read instead of listening to you.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: This capstone project asks you to choose a Tamil book or substantial text independently — perhaps a collection of Sangam poems, a modern novel, or a set of short stories — and read it closely over an extended period, applying everything learned this year. Afterward, you write a புத்தக மதிப்புரை (puthaga madhippurai, book report/review) that goes beyond a simple summary: briefly outline the கதைச்சுருக்கம் (plot) or content, identify the central கருப்பொருள் (theme), and offer your own reasoned personal response — what worked, what didn't, and why. A strong independent reading project also connects the chosen text to broader ideas studied this year, such as how it compares to classical literature, what its style reveals about its era, or how it reflects the culture and language you have been studying all along.
Let's practice what we just learned!
